content_voiceover: Let's talk about how we actually diagnose PNH in the lab. The classic older tests are the acid Ham test and the sucrose lysis test, or sugar water test, both of which lyse PNH red cells that have been exposed to activated complement. They're cheap, but they're labor intensive, insensitive, and not quantitative, so they're basically obsolete for board purposes. The modern gold standard is flow cytometry, which detects loss of GPI anchored proteins. On red cells you look at CD59 and CD55, and CD59 is actually better for distinguishing type two from type three PNH clones. On granulocytes you use CD59, CD55, CD24, CD16, and FLAER, which stands for fluorescently labeled inactive toxin aerolysin. FLAER binds directly to the GPI anchor itself, so it's more robust for clone size estimation, especially in granulocytes, because red cell measurements can underestimate clone size due to hemolysis. A key testable point, you need at least two antibodies to confirm the diagnosis, not just one, because CD59 and CD55 have different relative intensities on different cell lines, CD59 is brighter than CD55 on red cells, but dimmer than CD55 on white cells.
keypoints: Flow cytometry (CD59/CD55/FLAER) = gold standard, not Ham/sucrose lysis
Need ≥2 GPI-linked markers to confirm diagnosis
FLAER binds GPI anchor directly → best for clone size
CD59 > CD55 intensity on RBC; CD59 < CD55 on WBC
CD59 better distinguishes type II vs III clones
keypoint_voiceover: For boards, remember flow cytometry using GPI anchored proteins is the diagnostic gold standard for PNH, replacing the old Ham and sucrose lysis tests. You always need at least two antibodies, commonly CD59 and CD55, because their relative intensity flips between cell types, CD59 is brighter on red cells while CD55 is brighter on white cells. FLAER, which binds the GPI anchor directly, is the most robust marker for estimating clone size, particularly on granulocytes, since red cell based estimates tend to underestimate true clone size from ongoing hemolysis.
